clinicalPearls: Arterial (ischaemic) ulcers result from peripheral arterial disease causing tissue hypoperfusion, usually atherosclerotic, and when accompanied by rest pain or tissue loss they signify chronic limb-threatening ischaemia
They typically occur at the most distal or pressure-exposed sites, such as the toes, dorsum of the foot, heel, lateral malleolus and over bony prominences
The ulcer is classically punched-out with a well-defined edge, a pale or necrotic base with sparse granulation tissue and little exudate
Pain is prominent, worse on elevation and at night, and often relieved by hanging the leg dependently over the side of the bed

Examination reveals absent or diminished pulses, cool pale or dusky skin, hair loss, dependent rubor, prolonged capillary refill and a reduced ankle-brachial index, which may be falsely elevated where vessels are calcified
Assessment requires the ankle-brachial index, toe pressures and arterial duplex with cross-sectional or catheter angiography to define the level and severity of disease and revascularisation options

Healing depends on restoring perfusion, so revascularisation, whether endovascular or surgical bypass, is often required alongside risk-factor modification, antiplatelet and statin therapy, and smoking cessation
Compression bandaging is contraindicated in significant arterial disease, and dry ischaemic eschar should not be aggressively debrided until perfusion is addressed
reference.pathophysiology: Occlusive arterial disease, most often atherosclerosis, progressively reduces inflow to the distal limb. When resting perfusion falls below the metabolic demand of the tissues, the microcirculation can no longer sustain viability or support wound repair, so minor trauma at acral or pressure-bearing sites fails to heal and instead progresses to ulceration and necrosis. Impaired oxygen and nutrient delivery, endothelial dysfunction and a diminished capacity for angiogenesis mean the ulcer base remains poorly granulating and pale, and unless inflow is restored the deficit extends to frank gangrene.
additionalInvestigations: Arterial duplex ultrasound of the lower limb
CT or MR angiography, or catheter digital subtraction angiography, to plan revascularisation
Assessment of cardiovascular risk factors including lipid profile and glycaemic status
Wound tissue culture where infection is suspected
Transcutaneous oxygen pressure measurement where available to assess healing potential
redFlags: Ischaemic rest pain, gangrene or spreading tissue necrosis indicating a threatened limb
Signs of wound infection or sepsis superimposed on an ischaemic limb
A sudden cold, painful, pale, pulseless limb suggesting acute limb ischaemia
Rapidly progressive tissue loss despite treatment
reference.prognosis: Without revascularisation, arterial ulcers frequently fail to heal and may progress to gangrene and major amputation; timely restoration of perfusion improves limb salvage, but affected patients carry a high burden of coexisting cardiovascular disease and mortality.
pitfalls: Applying compression therapy to an arterial or mixed ulcer
Relying on the ankle-brachial index in calcified vessels where it may be falsely elevated
Debriding stable dry eschar before perfusion has been restored
Overlooking concurrent coronary and cerebrovascular disease
Delaying vascular referral in a patient with rest pain or tissue loss
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
European Society for Vascular Surgery guidelines on chronic limb-threatening ischaemia
NICE guidance on peripheral arterial disease
management: Revascularisation by endovascular angioplasty and stenting or surgical bypass to restore inflow is the definitive treatment
Cardiovascular risk factor modification with a statin, antiplatelet therapy, blood-pressure and glycaemic control, and smoking cessation
Wound care with non-adherent dressings, avoiding compression bandaging and avoiding debridement of dry stable eschar in ischaemic tissue
Effective analgesia for ischaemic rest pain
Prompt treatment of wound infection with culture-guided antibiotics
Foot protection, offloading of pressure areas and podiatry input
Amputation when the limb is unsalvageable or infection is uncontrolled, with vascular surgery referral and monitoring of healing
